To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“The Late Eocene and early Oligocene sedimentation of the Fayum, in the western Nile Valley in Egypt, records a major change from carbonate to clastic deposition that was caused by the initiation of drainage from the middle and East Africa, and the subsequent development of the Nile Valley.”

the Eocene sedimentary record of the Fayum, in Egypt, records the initiation of Nile drainage in Africa, and that the development of the modern Nile Valley was related to the uplift of the Red sea margin during the Oligocene.
the Nile River system began to flow northwards in the Eocene, and that this change was triggered by the onset of uplift in the East African Rift System.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the timing of the initiation of the Nile River and its drainage basin.
the timing, causes and consequences of the initiation of Nile drainage.
the evolution of drainage patterns in the Nile Basin, and the relationship between drainage and tectonics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Nile drainage was initiated in the Late Eocene, with the incised valley forming in the mid Miocene.
the Nile drainage system originated in the Late Eocene and was established by the Early Oligocene.
the Eocene initiation of Nile-type drainage in Egypt was caused by uplift in East Africa.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Nile drainage pattern has evolved over a long time period, from a system draining into the Red Sea to a system draining into Mediterranean Sea, and that this change in the Nile drainage pattern was controlled mainly by the tectonics of the East African Rift and the Red Sea Rift.

the Eocene initiation of the Nile drainage was due to the uplift in the Turkana area, which cut off the eastern drainage, and that the current route of Nile Valley was due to the Red Sea uplift in the Oligocene.

the Eocene-Oligocene boundary in the Fayum records the onset of a major tectono-eustatic cycle that led to the development of the current drainage pattern of the African continent and the formation of the Red Sea rift.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible, by careful integration of multiple lines of evidence, to reconstruct a detailed and accurate chronology of events in the geological record.
the Nile drainage system was not in its current configuration until the Messinian (5–6 Ma), and that the Nile Valley was not incised until then.

the modern drainage pattern of the Nile was initiated by a series of tectonic and climatic events that took place in the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene, and not, as previously thought, by the Miocene uplift of the Ethiopian highlands.
